Easy German Mushroom Sauce: (Quick Jägersauce Recipe)

ByGetty Stewart September 16, 2026September 17, 2026 September 17, 2026
Jump to Recipe Print Recipe
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:52
Instaread

If you have ever ordered Schnitzel at a traditional German restaurant, you already know the magic of Jägersauce. That rich, savoury mushroom gravy that elevates any dish. I learned how to make it the traditional way from my mom, who always started her sauce by rendering down smoky bacon fat and slowly sautéing fresh onions.

But I have a confession to make. As a kid, I never liked all the onions mom put in everything! So when I started cooking for myself, I made many dishes without onions. This mushroom gravy was one of them. I discovered that onion and garlic powder were a pretty good substitute and resulted in a much smoother sauce. Great flavour, smooth sauce and less work – that’s a win!

Also read: Spaetzle (German Noodles), German Creamy Cucumber Salad, Braised Red Cabbage

Now that I’m older, I actually like cooking with onions and garlic. But I still prefer the velvety texture that the powders provide. So while I gladly use fresh onions in my onion soup, sauteed mushroom and onions and cream of mushroom soup, onion powder remains my secret weapon for the ultimate smooth mushroom sauce.

What Is Jägersauce (Hunter Sauce)?

Jägersauce, sometimes spelled Jägersoße or jaeger sauce, literally means “hunter’s sauce” in English. It is a brown mushroom gravy from German and Austrian home cooking. The name comes from “Jäger,” the German word for hunter, since the sauce was traditionally served with game meat and wild mushrooms foraged from the forest by hunters.

Today, it’s best known as the sauce that often goes with schnitzel, hence the name, Jägerschnitzel. But in my family we have it with grilled or roasted meats or on top of mashed or boiled potatoes, rice or spätzle noodles. If you haven’t tried mushroom gravy with homemade German egg noodles (spätzle), you are missing out!

Fun Fact: The Delicious World of German Schnitzel

Did you know that Jägerschnitzel is just one option on a traditional German tavern menu? While they almost all start with a tender, juicy pork cutlet (or veal, in some cases), the name changes completely based on what you put on top:

  • Jägerschnitzel: Smothered in this rich, glossy brown mushroom gravy.
  • Rahmschnitzel: Topped with a luxurious, velvety decadent cream sauce.
  • Paprikaschnitzel: Smothered in a vibrant, smoky bell pepper and tomato sauce (sometimes called Zigeunerschnitzel or Balkan-style).
  • Zwiebelschnitzel: Piled high with sweet, deeply caramelized fried onions.
  • Wiener Schnitzel: The grandfather of them all! This version is kept completely plain, no sauce allowed, and is made traditionally from tender veal, and served simply with a lemon wedge to keep that beautiful breaded crust perfectly crispy. By the way, “Wiener” has nothing to do with hot dogs or sausages! It actually refers to “Wien,” the German word for Vienna, Austria’s capital city where this style originated. Literally translated, it means Vienna-style schnitzel.

I have tried them all. In all honesty, Jägerschnitzel continues to be my favourite to eat and to make.

Using Fresh Onions

Of course you can use fresh onions! My mom’s recipe and most traditional recipes for Jägersauce start with sautéing onions or shallots as the base before the mushrooms go in. It’s a good method that delivers real depth of flavour. Here’s what to do:

Sauté 1 small onion, finely diced or sliced (your choice), in butter or bacon fat until soft before searing the mushrooms. Add a clove of fresh, minced garlic near the end of cooking the mushrooms, it burns quickly so it’s the last thing to go in the pot.

Use the onion and garlic powder if you don’t love onion pieces in your gravy, you want the only texture to be mushrooms or you just can’t be bothered to chop onions.

Here’s a recap:

What Mushrooms Should You Use?

Cremini and white button mushrooms are both standard choices for Jägersauce, and either one works. Brown mushrooms (cremini) tend to have a slightly nuttier flavor and less water content than white button mushrooms, which means better browning and a bit more depth. But white mushrooms will work beautifully.

If you want to go a step further, and have a chance to forage for mushrooms, consider adding dried porcini (Steinpilze) or fresh chanterelles (Pfifferlinge) alongside the cremini. Even one or two added to the pot will add a little extra depth of flavour.

Can you use canned or jarred mushrooms?

Yes they’ll work in a pinch, but you’ll lose out on some of the flavour that comes with browning fresh mushrooms.

5 Foolproof Tips for a Perfectly Smooth Gravy

Serving lumpy Jägersauce is not an option! In addition to swapping out the onions and garlic for powder here are five more tips:

  1. Sauté and remove the mushrooms. Remove the mushrooms from the pan before making the roux. My mom and many experienced cooks will just make the roux with the mushrooms in the pan which works fine, especially if you’ve had as much practice as they have. If you’re just starting out, I highly recommend taking the mushrooms out of the pot to make it easier to incorporate all the flour properly.
  2. Use the correct ratio of fat, flour and liquid to make your roux. The general formula is:
    2 Tbsp fat + 2 Tbsp flour per 1 cup liquid
    Because our sauce has mushrooms and dehydrated onion powder that will both soak up liquid, we’re starting with 1 1/2 cups liquid in this particular recipe. It’s easier to add more liquid, so start with less and add more as needed.
  3. Use a whisk instead of spoon. A whisk helps to break up the flour better. You can switch to a wooden spoon once your sauce comes together.
  4. Add liquid gradually. Add a little broth at a time instead of adding it all at once. Add a small amount of broth and whisk it to make a smooth paste, drizzle in more liquid and keep whisking, repeat this until all the liquid has been incorporated and your sauce is the consistency you’d like.
  5. Don’t panic if a lump sneaks in. Even with all this care, lumps can happen. Keep whisking, most lumps smooth out as the sauce heats through. If a few stubborn ones stick around, pour the gravy through a fine mesh sieve before serving. No one will ever know.

What to Serve Jägersauce With

Jägersauce is meant to be served over something, and a few pairings show up again and again in German cooking:

  • Schnitzel is the classic pairing, whether pork, veal, or chicken.
  • Spätzle (German egg noodles) is the traditional starch, since the ridges hold onto the sauce well.
  • Mashed or pan-fried potatoes are just as common as spätzle.
  • French fries are a more casual match, especially alongside schnitzel.
  • Roasted or pan-seared meat, from pork roast to beef steak, takes well to the sauce too.

Pro Tip: For a vegetarian version, swap in oil or plant-based butter for the fat and vegetable broth instead of meat stock. Consider adding an extra splash of soy sauce, Worcestershire sauce (if fish is permitted) or mushroom powder for added depth of flavour.

How to Reheat Mushroom Sauce (Without It Separating)

This recipe uses a butter or bacon fat and flour roux, it will thicken significantly and turn jelly-like once it cools in the fridge. Don’t worry. This is completely normal!

You can reheat it and return it to normal, but you do need to do it carefully or your sauce could separate and look oily. This is especially true if you heat it too quickly or boil it too hard. Here’s what to do instead:

The Preferred Method: On the Stovetop

  1. Transfer your leftover mushroom gravy into a small saucepan.
  2. Add 1 to 2 tablespoons of beef broth (or water) to help loosen the starch bonds.
  3. Turn the heat to low.
  4. Whisk constantly as the pan warms up. As the starch melts and absorbs the fresh liquid, the gravy will smoothly return to its original velvety consistency.
  5. Once it is hot and bubbling gently, remove it from the heat and serve.

The Quick Method: In the Microwave

If you are short on time, you can use the microwave, but you must do it in short bursts:

  1. Place the gravy in a microwave-safe bowl and add a tiny splash of broth or water.
  2. Cover the bowl with a paper towel to trap the steam.
  3. Microwave on medium power for 30 seconds, then take it out and give it a vigorous whisk.
  4. Repeat in 15-second intervals, whisking between each round, until it is hot and completely smooth.

Recipe for German Mushroom Sauce (Jaeger Sauce)

Print Recipe
No ratings yet

German Mushroom Sauce or Jaeger Sauce

A quick and easy German mushroom sauce or Jaeger sauce. Using onion and garlic powder instead of fresh aromatics keeps the sauce smooth while adding plenty of flavour. Serve with schnitzel, pork, chicken, mashed potatoes or noodles.
Prep : 10 minutes mins
Cook : 20 minutes mins
Total Time: 30 minutes mins
Servings: 4
Author: Getty Stewart

Ingredients

  • 8 oz cremini or button mushrooms, sliced 225 g
  • 3 Tbsp butter or bacon fat divided
  • 1 tsp onion powder
  • 1/4 tsp garlic powder
  • 2 Tbsp all-purpose flour
  • 1 ½ cups beef broth or vegetable
  • 1/2 tsp soy sauce
  • 1/2 tsp apple cider vinegar or lemon juice or white wine
  • Salt and black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • Heat 1 tablespoon of butter (or bacon fat) in large sauce pan over medium-high heat.
  • Add mushrooms and cook without stirring too much until they release their moisture and turn deeply golden, 8 to 10 minutes.
  • Sprinkle onion powder and garlic powder over mushrooms at last minute and stir to coat. Remove mushrooms from pot. Set aside.
  • Melt remaining 2 tablespoons of butter (or bacon fat) in same pan over medium heat. Keep any leftover bits or fond in the pan to build flavour. Sprinkle flour over melted fat and whisk constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, until mixture turns lightly golden and smells nutty.
  • Slowly pour in 1/2 cup broth whisking constantly to form a paste and scrape off any browned bits on bottom of pan. Continue adding broth a little at a time, whisking constantly to thin out the paste into a smooth, even liquid. Repeat as needed until all broth has been incorporated and you get the desired consistency. You want a smooth pourable gravy that coats the back of a spoon.
  • Bring mixture to a gentle bubble, reduce heat to medium-low and simmer for 5 minutes.
  • Add mushrooms to sauce and let warm through. Remove from heat, add the vinegar or lemon juice, taste and season as needed.

Notes

Fresh Onion Version: Slice onions thinly and mince garlic. Sauté onions for 5-8 minutes over medium heat. They should be soft and transparent, be careful not to brown them. Add mushrooms and cook as described. Add garlic at the very end cooking just until aromatic. Remove everything from pan before making roux.
Gluten Free: To make this gluten free omit the flour. After sautéing mushrooms add broth and seasoning, stir in a cornstarch slurry made with one tablespoon of cornstarch dissolved in 2 tablespoons of water and simmer for a minute until thickened.  
Vegetarian Version: Replace butter or bacon fat with oil or plant-based butter and use vegetable broth.
